findings.title: Device limit is bypassed after the first rejected request due to localCache set before the DB call
findings.body: In tagDeviceUI, localCache.SetDefault(key, ...) is executed before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device ID is still marked as tagged in the 29-minute local cache. On the user's next request, the cache hit makes tagDeviceUI return nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. The net effect is that the device limit only rejects each new device once per ~29 minutes; every subsequent request from that device authenticates successfully. The cache entry must only be set after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (and any error path should invalidate it).

findings.title: Count-then-insert race allows the device limit to be exceeded
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices in one session and, if the count is below deviceLimit, performs the insert in a separate session/transaction. Two (or many) concurrent requests from different new devices can each observe count < limit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-insert must be atomic (e.g. a single conditional insert/transaction with a lock, or a unique count constraint) to actually enforce the limit under load, which is exactly the scenario (burst of anonymous requests) this feature targets.

findings.title: TagDevice moved onto the synchronous request path, removing the previous timeout/async isolation
findings.body: The old code ran TagDevice in a goroutine with a 2-minute context.WithTimeout, so database slowness in the anon_device table never delayed or failed anonymous authentication. The new code calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...) synchronously inside Authenticate using the request context. Now every anonymous request performs up to two extra DB round trips (COUNT + INSERT/UPDATE) before the identity is returned; a slow or locked anon_device table will hang or fail all anonymous access. If the synchronous behavior is required to surface the limit error, consider at minimum retaining a timeout so DB issues cannot degrade anonymous auth.

findings.title: ErrDeviceLimitReached returned raw from Authenticate produces an opaque 500-style auth failure
findings.body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate returns that error directly. The authn layer will treat this as an internal authentication error rather than an expected 'too many devices' condition, so users over the limit will get a generic error (likely 500 Internal Server Error on every request) with no indication of the cause. There is no mapping of this sentinel error to an appropriate HTTP status (e.g. 403/429) or user-facing message anywhere in this PR, making the feature effectively brick anonymous access without explanation once the limit is hit (combined with the cache bug, intermittently).

findings.title: MySQL rowsAffected==0 misinterpreted as device-limit-reached
findings.body: updateDevice treats result.RowsAffected() == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. With MySQL's default behavior (rows affected = rows *changed*, not rows matched), an UPDATE that sets identical values reports 0 affected rows. updated_at has second precision in MySQL, so an update of an existing device within the same second (or with unchanged values) can yield 0 rows affected and wrongly return ErrDeviceLimitReached, rejecting a legitimate existing device. The code should distinguish 'device row not found/not active' from 'no values changed' (e.g. check for existence separately or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS semantics).

findings.title: Expiry window logic: a device that exists but is older than 30 days can never be updated when limit is reached, and error semantics conflate cases
findings.body: updateDevice's WHERE clause requires updated_at BETWEEN (UpdatedAt-30d) and (UpdatedAt+1m). If the count of active devices has reached the limit but the requesting device's row exists yet falls outside that window (e.g. clock skew or a device idle just past 30 days before cleanup runs), the UPDATE affects 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached even though this device is one of the 'expired' rows that shouldn't count toward the limit. The store then neither updates nor deletes the stale row, so the device stays locked out until the 61-day cleanup job removes it.

findings.title: AnonymousDeviceLimit exposed to all frontend clients including anonymous users
findings.body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is included in the frontend settings DTO served to every requester, including unauthenticated/anonymous visitors. This leaks an instance's configured capacity limit (useful reconnaissance for abuse: an attacker knows exactly how many spoofed X-Grafana-Device-Id values are needed to lock out legitimate anonymous users, since the limit is enforced per arbitrary client-supplied device IDs). Consider only exposing it to signed-in admins, or not exposing it at all if no frontend code consumes it — no frontend usage is added in this PR, only the type declarations.

findings.title: New device_limit setting is undocumented and lacks validation
findings.body: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting is parsed with MustInt64(0) but has no documentation (configure docs/conf defaults), and negative values are not rejected. A negative value behaves like 0 (limit disabled) due to the `deviceLimit > 0` check, silently ignoring the user's intent; a validation error for negative values would be clearer. Also note that device_limit interacts with the 61-day retention (keepFor) in impl.go while the limit counts only devices active in the last 30 days — this asymmetry is nowhere documented for operators.
